title: Claude-powered trading agent for Robinhood/Public — solved the plumbing, still can't solve edge
author: BFitch85
selftext:
I've spent the last few months building an agent that runs Claude against my own brokerage account. The engineering side is genuinely finished and works. The part I can't crack is the part that actually matters: whether any of it has edge.

Quick disclosure so nobody feels misled, this did turn into a product I sell. I'm not linking it and I'm not here to pitch; I'm here because the strategy problem has me stuck and this sub knows more about it than I do. Mods, happy to remove if that's still not allowed.

What's actually built:

Desktop app, runs on my own machine. Connects to Robinhood's agentic API and Public's REST API, my credentials are encrypted locally by the OS and never leave the machine. Strategies are written in plain English rather than code, so changing a rule means editing a sentence.

Every cycle, the agent pulls quotes, option chains, historicals, earnings dates and technical indicators, then proposes a trade with its reasoning attached. Nothing reaches the broker without me clicking through a review-then-confirm gate. There's an autonomous mode, but the guardrails still apply when it's on: per-trade cap, daily trade limit, total exposure cap, market-hours restriction, a daily-loss circuit breaker, and an automatic stop-loss attached to every position it opens. Kill switch on the desktop and on my phone.

There's a paper mode that simulates fills against live quotes through the identical pipeline, same agent, same guardrails, same approvals, no real orders. Plus backtesting, a P&L ledger with per-strategy attribution, and a full audit log of every tool call the agent made.

Where I'm stuck:

Same wall a lot of people here describe. The infrastructure is solid and the agent reliably does what I tell it, but "what I tell it" is a paragraph of plain English I wrote, and I have no principled way to know if that paragraph is any good. I can see exactly what it did and why, and I still can't tell whether a losing stretch means the strategy is wrong, the market changed, or it's just variance over too few trades.

The returns have been green but modest over the course of a months testing, but the negative swings were large at first, before I implemented an auto-stop to each order the agent places itself.

Things I've genuinely learned the hard way, in case they're useful to anyone:

Feeding the agent its own past reasoning made it worse. Previous stand-downs and losses coloured every subsequent decision. It reasons better fresh each cycle from the account snapshot and live data.

It'll silently reason around missing data rather than telling you it's missing. I had a strategy referencing a position-age field that didn't exist on one of the two code paths, and nothing errored, it just quietly worked around it for weeks.

Most of my API cost was one tool. Historical bars were \~25% of calls and dominated the payload; trimming what came back cut the bill substantially with no loss of signal.

What I'm asking:

How do you actually develop and validate edge for something like this? Specifically: how many trades before a strategy's results mean anything? How do you separate "this doesn't work" from "this hasn't had enough sample"? And is a plain-English strategy fundamentally limited compared to a coded one, or is that a red herring?

EDIT - stack, since people asked on similar posts:

Electron desktop app, Node/JS. Robinhood agentic API + Public REST. Claude via the Anthropic API, I pay my own token costs, typically a few dollars a day. Small Node licensing server on a DigitalOcean droplet. Everything runs locally; no trading logic on any server I control.

comments.author: VisibleAirport2996
comments.body: Do you understand how claude and other llms work?

replies.author: BFitch85
replies.body:
Well enough to know it's a next-token predictor with no price model, no market state, and no memory between runs. That's not a knock, it's why the system is built the way it is.

It isn't asked to predict anything. It's asked to fetch data through tools, apply rules I wrote in plain English, and produce a proposal with its reasoning. Every action is gated by code, caps, limits, a circuit breaker, an approval click. The model can't place an order; it can only suggest one.

And it's exactly why the post says I can't demonstrate edge. I'm not claiming an LLM sees something in a chart that a human doesn't. If you think the whole approach is doomed for reasons beyond that, I'd genuinely rather hear it than not, that's more useful to me than agreement.

replies.author: VisibleAirport2996
replies.body: Then you’ve built the edge, the agent execution/interpretation, what’s missing is the human input or out of box thinking to come up with a trade. As you notice past lessons make the LLM worse, rather than learning from mistakes it is “selecting” the next best prediction.

replies.author: BFitch85
replies.body:
Better way of putting it than I managed. That's the trap with "learning from mistakes", nothing in a context window updates weights. Past reasoning is just more tokens shaping the next output, so a run of losses doesn't teach caution, it makes cautious-sounding text more likely. Looks like learning right up until it stands down on a setup it took fine last week.

Wouldn't call the execution layer edge though. It stops me wrecking a decent idea with bad discipline, but a disciplined system running a bad idea still loses, just tidier.

How do you handle the idea side? Deriving rules yourself, or is there a process for finding setups in the first place?

comments.author: vitholomewjenkins
comments.body: Have your AI write your strategy as a python script, that way it’s structurally secure & keeps the ai from straying the path.

replies.author: BFitch85
replies.body:
Guardrails are already code on my side. Caps, daily limits, exposure, circuit breaker, auto stop attached to every fill. The model can't place an order at all, it can only propose one and I click. So I think the structural part is covered.

Where I'm less sure is the strategy itself. If I code the setup logic fully then I've basically built a normal algo bot and the LLM isn't earning its place. The reason it's prose is so it can weigh stuff that doesn't fit neatly in a rule, like earnings timing or how the move actually developed on the day.

Good point on reproducibility though. It's got a set list of tools to call from, but the logs show it calling them differently run to run on similar setups. Same paragraph, different read. That's probably a big part of why I can't separate a bad strategy from a small sample.

Have you gone full script yourself? Curious whether you kept any judgment layer or cut it out completely.

replies.author: BFitch85
replies.body:
Yep, it's in the post, second paragraph.   
Not linking it and not here to pitch. I'm stuck on the strategy side and this sub knows more about that than I do.

comments.author: 206throw
comments.body: you built the easy part, the hard part is picking a strategy that is profitable when you run it live with commission costs etc.  Suggest to go look up proven strategies pick one that is simple and then test it on a paper account and then test another one then repeat.

replies.author: BFitch85
replies.body:
Fair. And the cost point is where I've been sloppy, my paper mode fills at the mark and doesn't model the bid/ask spread at all, so anything I test there is flattering by however wide the spread was. On options that's a bigger drag than fees.

The one at a time and repeat part is what I needed to hear. I've been changing the strategy while changing other things at the same time, so I can't attribute results to anything.

On proven strategies, do you find published ones still hold up, or do you use them as a starting shape and adapt? My assumption is anything documented well enough to find is already crowded, but I'd rather be wrong about that.

replies.author: 206throw
replies.body: For me the trading concept was figured out probably over 100 years ago but I have 150+ code releases trying to get the entry point dialed in etc.  So even if the concept was figured out the execution has to be figured out.
